assessments.known_bound: Verified for all n ≤ 10^18 (reduces to primes); true unless n ≡ one of 198 bad classes mod 120120 (Terzi); exceptions in [1,x] ≤ x·exp(-c(log x)^{2/3}) (Vaughan)
routes: Reduce to prime n via scaling 4/p = 1/x+1/y+1/z ⇒ 4/(mp) = 1/(mx)+1/(my)+1/(mz)
Parametric identities for n even, n ≡ 3 mod 4, n ≡ 2 mod 3, n ≡ 0 mod 3 via field_simp; ring, splitting 1/a = 1/(a+1)+1/(a(a+1)) for distinctness
Obláth: n+1 divisible by a prime ≡ 3 mod 4 gives a solution; Mordell's identities cover all but {1,121,169,289,361,529} mod 840
Full conjecture (residues like n ≡ 1 mod 24) has no known proof; negation is false up to 10^18 so no counterexample search is viable
assessments.rationale: This is the open Erdős–Straus conjecture: a universal statement unprovable in full by current mathematics and with no findable counterexample (verified to 10^18), so only partial residue-class results are formalizable and budget should be minimal.

assessments.known_bound: Verified for all n ≤ 10^18 (MiDu25); true unless n ≡ {1,121,169,289,361,529} mod 840 (Mordell); exceptions ≤ x·exp(-c(log x)^{2/3}) (Vaughan)

assessments.known_bound: Hindman's theorem (1974): holds for any finite number of colours; Mathlib has Hindman.exists_FS_of_finite_cover via idempotent ultrafilters
routes: Apply Hindman.exists_FS_of_finite_cover in ℕ+ to the cover {n | c n = i}, get a stream a with FS a ⊆ colour class; extract strictly increasing block-sum stream b with FS b ⊆ FS a; take A = range of b and show every nonempty finite subset sum of A lies in FS b
Same start, but extract a strictly increasing subsequence of FS-values via Hindman.FS.add / FS_iter_tail_sub_FS recursively instead of block grouping
Direct Galvin–Glazer proof via an idempotent ultrafilter on ℕ+ (Hindman.FS_partition_regular packaging), then same set-extraction step
assessments.rationale: The core theorem is already in Mathlib (Hindman), so the work is a nontrivial but routine transfer from streams/FS to an infinite set of positive integers with all nonempty finite subset sums monochromatic.

assessments.known_bound: k = 2, N = 0 works: 2*(n+2) - (2 + (n+2)) = n for all n >= 0 (Seamans)

assessments.rationale: The frozen statement lets us choose k, so the explicit witness k=2, N=0, a=![2, n+2] closes it in a few tactic lines.

routes: Exhibit Ko's witness x=2^12*3^6, y=2^8*3^8, z=2^11*3^7 and prove an abstract lemma (a^12 b^6)^x (a^8 b^8)^y = (a^11 b^7)^z from linear exponent identities 12x+8y=11z, 6x+8y=7z via mul_pow/pow_mul/pow_add

assessments.rationale: Existence claim with a known explicit witness; the only difficulty is avoiding kernel evaluation of the astronomically large powers, handled by keeping exponents symbolic until the final exact.

assessments.rationale: Explicit Ko-type witness is known and the proof is a short structural rewrite on exponents, provided no tactic tries to evaluate the astronomically large powers.

assessments.known_bound: Brown–Landman 1999: monochromatic 3-AP with d > f(x) for any increasing f; Alweiss short argument (eventual constancy)
routes: Alweiss argument: WLOG c 1 = red; AP (1,3,5) forces 3 or 5 blue; Case 3 blue: for n≥6 red n ⇒ 2n−1 blue ⇒ n+1 red, so c eventually constant on [N,∞), witness (N, N+1); Case 5 blue: for n≥9 red n ⇒ n+2 red, so c eventually constant on odd numbers ≥ N, witness (N, 2N) with N odd
Handle WLOG by proving a lemma for arbitrary c under hypothesis c 1 = true, then apply to c and to fun n => !c n

Compactness/finite route: find minimal M such that every 2-colouring of {1..M} has such a 3-AP (small backtracking search), then decide over Fin M → Bool via decide/native_decide and lift to ℕ by restriction
Induction bookkeeping via Nat.le_induction and omega for all AP arithmetic; avoid ℕ subtraction by writing third term as 1 + 2*(n-1) or reparametrising n = k+1
assessments.rationale: Resolved for-all statement with a known short case-analysis proof (Alweiss) that is directly formalizable with Nat.le_induction and omega, plus a finite decide fallback.

assessments.known_bound: Disproved: A = {(n+1)! + n : n ≥ 0} is Sidon and meets every infinite AP (Baumgartner 1975 implicit; AlphaProof explicit witness, Lean-verified)
routes: Explicit witness A = range (fun n => (n+1)! + n): Sidon via 2·f(i) < f(j) for i<j (lacunary), AP-hitting via d ∣ (a+d+1)! with n = a+d and t = (a+d+1)!/d + 1
Lacunary principle: any strictly increasing f with f(n+1) > 2 f(n) gives a Sidon range; prove growth lemma with Nat.factorial_succ + nlinarith, injectivity via strictMono_nat_of_lt_succ
Sidon case analysis: rcases lt_trichotomy on max indices j vs l, close impossible cases by omega/linarith using the auxiliary doubling inequality, then cancel and use injectivity
Alternative witness {⌊x^n⌋} (Dutta) or greedy Baumgartner enumeration — harder to formalize, avoid
assessments.rationale: Resolved disproof with a known explicit factorial witness; the formalization is elementary but needs careful handling of the Sidon case split and factorial divisibility, so a construct-mode medium budget suffices.

assessments.known_bound: Sándor 1997: proper divisors of 120 (excl. 1) are a counterexample, reciprocal sum 239/120 < 2; minimal counterexample {2,3,4,5,6,7,10,11,13,14,15} (Stobart)
routes: Witness A = divisors of 120 in [2,60]; scale by 120: each subset's reciprocal sum ×120 is a natural number, so <1 forces ≤119; but total is 239 > 238, contradiction via omega
Prove lemma (∑ n∈B, 1/n)*120 = (∑ n∈B, 120/n : ℕ) for B ⊆ A pointwise, then Finset.sum_sdiff to split total 239 and finish with Nat.cast_lt + omega
Brute force: witness Stobart's 11-element set and decide over all 2^11 subsets in ℚ — heavier for kernel, fallback only
assessments.rationale: Disproved problem with an explicit 14-element witness whose verification reduces to an integer parity/counting argument (239 ≤ 238 impossible) needing no subset enumeration.

assessments.known_bound: Sándor 1997: proper divisors of 120 (14 elements) are a counterexample; minimal counterexample {2,3,4,5,6,7,10,11,13,14,15} (Stobart)
routes: Witness A = proper divisors of 120 minus {1}; sum = 239/120 < 2; integrality: 120*sum over any subset is a natural number, so each part < 1 forces 120*part <= 119, total <= 238 < 239, contradiction
Witness Stobart set {2,3,4,5,6,7,10,11,13,14,15}; exhaustive 2^11 subset check over ℚ via decide/native_decide that no subset sum lies in the window making both parts < 1
Hybrid: use the 120 witness but discharge the subset-sum contradiction by decide over 2^14 subsets (heavier; prefer integrality argument)
assessments.rationale: Explicit known counterexample with a one-paragraph integrality proof (all reciprocals are multiples of 1/120), so only witness construction plus routine casting/sum-splitting lemmas are needed.

assessments.known_bound: Explicit infinite family (Somani): for a>=2, c=8a^2+8a+1, cb(a)cb(2a+2)cb(c)=cb(a+1)cb(2a)cb(c+1)
routes: Witness family a ↦ ({a,2a+2,c},{a+1,2a,c+1}) with c=8a^2+8a+1; prove membership via Nat.succ_mul_centralBinom_succ applied at a,2a,2a+1,c, clear K=(a+1)(2a+1)(2a+2)(c+1) and cancel with Nat.centralBinom_pos
Infinitude via Set.infinite_of_injective_forall_mem with the map a+2 ↦ pair (injective since a is the min of the first finset / omega on Finset ext), or via Set.infinite_of_not_bddAbove on an image

assessments.rationale: Known explicit infinite family with a straightforward but fiddly Lean proof (Finset literal products, ratio lemma four times, cancellation, injectivity), so a construct-mode medium budget suffices.

assessments.known_bound: Disproved: infinitely many collections with all |I_i|=4 for every n=3 and n>=4 (Ulas 2005, Bauer–Bennett 2007); also |I_i|=5, n>=5 (Bennett–van Luijk 2012).
routes: Erdős-style pigeonhole: for fixed N take blocks [x,x+3] with x≡1 mod 4, N<x≤4m; map subsets S to the parity vector of the factorization of ∏f(x) over primes <4m+4; when |X|>π'(4m+4) (bound π' via Nat.primeCounting'_add_le with a=210, φ(210)=48) two subsets collide and S△T ≠ ∅ has square product, all starts >N ⇒ infinitely many collections

Same pigeonhole but avoid prime counting: use the coarser bound that the number of primes below 4m+4 is at most the number of odd numbers plus 1 and take blocks of length 4 starting at x≡1 mod 4 in a range whose size exceeds that — density check fails (1/4 < 1/2), so needs at least the mod-210 sieve or a smarter block choice (e.g. only blocks whose entries are all composite-heavy) — fallback only
Explicit Pell/elliptic-curve families (Ulas; Bauer–Bennett) — infinite parametric solutions to (A²−1)(B²−1)=□ realized as x²+3x+1 — hard to formalize, not recommended

Reduce infinitude of the Finset-of-Finsets set to a min-start-exceeds-N statement via Set.infinite_of_not_bddAbove-style argument on sup of the starts, or by injecting an infinite family of pairwise distinct collections
assessments.rationale: The negation is a genuine infinite-family statement with no bounded computation; the elementary pigeonhole-on-parity-vectors route is provable in Mathlib but requires nontrivial bookkeeping (factorization parity, prime-counting bound via φ(210)=48, disjointness, and translating to Set.Infinite of Finset (Finset ℕ)).

assessments.known_bound: A = ℕ, g(n) = n+1 gives the set = ℕ, lower and upper density both 1
routes: Witness A = Set.univ, g n = n+1; show Nat.card {p : univ × univ // p.1+p.2 = n} = n+1 via equivalence with Finset.Nat.antidiagonal n (card_antidiagonal), so the defining set is all of ℕ
Then {n ∈ Iio N ∧ ...} = Iio N, ncard = N, ratio eventually equals 1 for N ≥ 1; conclude liminf = 1 via Tendsto.liminf_eq (tendsto_const_nhds.congr') and 0 < 1
Alternative: use Filter.liminf_congr with an EventuallyEq to constant 1 plus Filter.liminf_const, avoiding Tendsto machinery
If the Nat.card of the subtype is awkward, build the Equiv {p : univ×univ // ...} ≃ Fin (n+1) directly via p ↦ p.1 and Nat.card_eq_fintype_card / Fintype.card_fin
assessments.rationale: Trivial explicit counterexample (A = ℕ, g = n+1) already noted on the site; the only work is Lean plumbing for Nat.card of the antidiagonal subtype and the eventually-constant liminf.
